TL;DR: CASP enhances NP-hard optimization by verifying predictions with a polynomial-time verifier, ensuring correctness without relying on prediction quality. It offers learnable certificate parameters and shows improved performance over unverified methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of machine-learned predictions in NP-hard optimization by ensuring correctness through verification rather than reliance on the predictions themselves.

Method: CASP utilizes a polynomial-time verifier to assess which parts of the search space can be ignored, maintaining correctness independent of the predictor's output quality.

Result: The study reveals that verified deployment of predictions maintains optimal solutions, while unverified approaches can lead to significant losses under distribution shifts, quantifying the advantages of the verification process.

Conclusion: Verified predictions improve optimization outcomes significantly compared to unverified methods, demonstrating the importance of sound verification in machine learning applications for NP-hard problems.

Abstract: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

</details>


### [246] [Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14563)
*Tatthapong Srikitrungruang,Jaesung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework to estimate elastic properties from low-resolution data amidst noise, enhancing robustness through a novel approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges of estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution measurements, especially in the presence of noise and resolution degradation.

Method: The PIE-PINN framework combines displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals modeled via Laplace distributions, utilizing a B-spline-guided displacement network and a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for improved error scaling.

Result: The framework demonstrates increased robustness in recovering Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy data across various noise levels and observation resolutions.

Conclusion: PIE-PINN effectively enhances the estimation of elastic properties by adaptively downweighting errors and providing a unified probabilistic modeling approach.

Abstract: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse elasticity problem because low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneous property variations, and small measurement perturbations or fitting errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing inverse methods often rely on high-fidelity observations and manually prespecified loss weights, limiting their adaptability and making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. We propose a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework for robust estimation of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data. PIE-PINN models displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. To improve robustness, the framework combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global representation of the displacement field, while the neural network correction captures local variations. The hierarchical scale model adaptively downweights severe displacement fitting errors, enabling more robust recovery of the latent mean displacement field. An alternating maximum-likelihood training strategy updates the mean through weighted residual minimization and updates the scales to adjust the loss weights. Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate the robustness of PIE-PINN.

</details>


### [247] [Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14571)
*Dante Lok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents gate-zero growth, a novel FP operator for continual learning that maintains old knowledge while adding new functionalities through a zero-initialised gate structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study addresses the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning by introducing a method that preserves old functions while enabling the addition of new ones.

Method: Gate-zero growth utilizes a zero-initialised gate that, under certain conditions, leads to rank separation in the functional Jacobian, enabling controlled functional variation as new weights are added.

Result: Experiments on a substantial Transformer model demonstrate that gate-zero growth achieves minimal forgetting of old knowledge while other non-FP methods exhibit significantly larger forgetting rates.

Conclusion: The findings establish gate-zero growth as a structured approach to continual learning, presenting a framework that can enhance knowledge retention in machine learning models.

Abstract: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

</details>


### [248] [Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14576)
*Hyemin Gu,Michael Tyrrell,Tuhin Sahai,Markos A. Katsoulakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the sublinear-growth principle for deep residual architectures, establishing a stability threshold for residual block velocity fields where the input-magnitude exponent must not exceed 1 to ensure stable training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify and formalize the conditions under which deep residual architectures can be trained safely without instability caused by excessive velocity field growth.

Method: The analysis combines classical ODE theory and optimal control via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to derive stability criteria at the level of residual block architecture.

Result: The threshold for stable training is found at the input-magnitude exponent q = 1, ensuring stable operation under this condition while also providing guidelines for architectural design to maintain stability.

Conclusion: The exponent criterion q ≤ 1 is essential for ensuring stability in training and inference, and the proposed modifications effectively enforce this condition in practical neural architectures.

Abstract: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

</details>


### [249] [Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14607)
*Umid Suleymanov,Ilhama Novruzova,Khalid Mammadov,Natavan Hasanova,Murat Kantarcioglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study investigates how fairness interventions in machine learning affect privacy risks, revealing that the impact varies by model architecture and subgroup characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the interplay between fairness-enhancing algorithms and privacy risks in machine learning models used in sensitive sectors.

Method: Adaptation of the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing and analysis of the interaction between Differential Privacy (DP) and fairness methods.

Result: Privacy disparities were uncovered, showing that fairness interventions have varying effects on privacy risks based on multiple factors.

Conclusion: Fairness, privacy, and utility should be jointly assessed at the subpopulation level, supported by a new empirical auditing framework.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

</details>


### [250] [Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14613)
*Jin Dai,Qiuzhen Zhang,Chenyun Dai,Danmei Lan,Can Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study presents Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) to enhance ECG arrhythmia diagnosis in long-tailed label distributions. AG-SCL features a contrastive learning approach, adaptive logit adjustment, and tailored augmentation, achieving superior performance on ECG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-tailed label distributions hinder accurate ECG arrhythmia diagnosis, especially for rare but critical abnormalities. Existing techniques fail to account for morphological variability within ECG classes.

Method: AG-SCL comprises three components: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch for class uncertainty, Adaptive Logit Adjustment for specific prior corrections, and tail-aware augmentation to preserve morphology in ECG data.

Result: AG-SCL outperformed existing methods on the PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset, achieving balanced accuracy and sensitivity improvements, particularly in rare classes.

Conclusion: AG-SCL enhances long-tailed ECG diagnosis through combined calibration and representation learning, improving detection of rare arrhythmias without sacrificing specificity.

Abstract: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets. On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

</details>


### [251] [Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14614)
*Weiwen Xu,Jia Liu,Hou Pong Chan,Long Li,Deng Cai,Min Chen,Hao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO) as an advanced method for reinforcement learning that improves reward shaping by using token-level contrastive disagreement to distinguish beneficial uncertainty from confusion, leading to better performance compared to traditional entropy-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The limitation of traditional reinforcement learning reward shaping methods, which use entropy and fail to effectively differentiate useful uncertainty from confusion.

Method: Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO) uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for advantage shaping in reinforcement learning.

Result: CPO demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional entropy-based RLVR methods across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, and effectively resolves the zero-advantage problem.

Conclusion: By balancing correct and incorrect responses in its evaluation strategy, CPO achieves enhanced exploration and exploitation, resulting in optimal performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

</details>


### [252] [TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14640)
*Wen Yang Tan,Jiawei Li,Fang Liu,Wei Zhang,Sumei Sun,Peng Cheng Wang,Elisa Y. M. Ang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents TIDE, a battery degradation estimator focused on accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability for better battery health management in connected systems, achieving significant estimation improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate battery health estimation is crucial for management in connected devices, as erroneous states can negatively impact system control and longevity.

Method: TIDE integrates battery-domain knowledge with operational data using a three-component backbone: a knowledge-guided degradation prior for trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual for consistent interpretation, and a contextual learning component for accuracy.

Result: TIDE enhances estimation accuracy by an average of 19.7% over benchmarks, reduces aging inconsistencies, and supports both component-level and model-level interpretations.

Conclusion: The TIDE framework effectively improves battery health monitoring and decision support, making it applicable for intelligent connected systems.

Abstract: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

</details>


### [253] [Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14652)
*Shusheng Xiao,Jinshuai Bai,Hyogu Jeong,Yunfei Xi,Yilin Gui,YuanTong Gu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework that enables efficient conditional topology generation while maintaining structural feasibility and physical consistency, outperforming traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for efficient design exploration in topology optimisation due to repeated analysis and sensitivity updates, especially when multiple designs are required under varying conditions.

Method: The study develops FMTO using a trajectory-aware formulation that combines Gaussian field interpolation with mechanically meaningful states derived from the BESO method, optimizing without additional inference-time constraints.

Result: FMTO produces diverse topologies with enhanced compliance performance, satisfaction of volume-fraction constraints, and improved topology fidelity, requiring fewer sampling steps compared to diffusion-based methods.

Conclusion: With limited training data and moderate trajectory weighting, the FMTO framework offers superior performance in generating topologies, indicating its potential for broader applications beyond two dimensions.

Abstract: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

</details>


### [254] [Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14672)
*Yusuke Sakemi,Tomoya Takeuchi,Takeo Hosomi,Kazuyuki Aihara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a memory-efficient training framework for deep continuous-time spiking neural networks using differentiable spike-time discretization, enhancing training speed and reducing memory requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the memory constraints of training deep continuous-time spiking neural networks, particularly with exact spike-time computation.

Method: A memory-efficient approach called differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) is introduced, which replaces variable candidate firing times with fixed intervals while preserving membrane-potential dynamics. It also implements temporal regularization inspired by synfire chains.

Result: DSTD significantly reduces memory consumption and training time, achieving a reduction of up to 100-fold in memory and 20-fold in training time, thereby enabling training of deeper SNNs.

Conclusion: The proposed framework allows successful training of deep spiking neural networks on standard datasets using limited computational resources.

Abstract: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware. However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

</details>


### [255] [Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14705)
*Yuchang Zhu,Zezhong Xie,Huizhe Zhang,Huazhen Zhong,Jintang Li,Liang Chen,Zibin Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses group fairness in graph neural networks (GNNs) without relying on demographic information, proposing a method called Grad2Fair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to improve fairness in GNNs while not making strong assumptions about the availability of demographic data.

Method: The authors introduce GradDist, a metric based on gradient distributions of misclassified nodes to quantify bias, and Grad2Fair, a method that uses gradients to achieve fairness without demographic predictions.

Result: Experiments on various real-world datasets show that Grad2Fair outperforms existing baselines in terms of fairness and classification performance.

Conclusion: Grad2Fair effectively mitigates bias in GNNs without requiring demographic information, ensuring more stable fairness outcomes.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

</details>


### [256] [MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14706)
*Xin Li,Zixin Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MESHA is a proposed algorithm for Best Arm Identification in strategic linear bandits, which effectively counters strategic misreporting by arms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle the challenges posed by arms in strategic linear bandits that may misreport features to appear as the best options in Best Arm Identification.

Method: The algorithm incorporates naive uniform sampling and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition to mitigate the effects of strategic behaviors and verify arm reports against true features.

Result: Proven that any arm will aim to pass the Grim Trigger Condition under any Nash Equilibrium, establishing an upper bound on the failure probability within a set budget.

Conclusion: Numerical experiments show MESHA surpasses existing optimal design algorithms in handling strategic misreporting, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Abstract: We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

</details>


### [257] [BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15207)
*Qi Li,Xingyi Yang,Xinchao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces BadWAM, a framework for evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks on World-Action Models (WAMs), showing their vulnerability to adversarial attacks that misalign imagined and executed actions, affecting task success rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore the robustness and interpretability of World-Action Models by checking robotic actions against their imagined futures.

Method: Introduced BadWAM to model World-Action Drift Attacks, characterized by attack strength and stealthiness, presenting two attack types: action-only and imagination-preserving.

Result: Evaluation revealed substantial reductions in task success rates for both attack types, with the action-only attack dropping success from 96.5% to 43.1%.

Conclusion: Moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain high attack performance while reducing the drift between imagined and executed actions.

Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

</details>


### [258] [Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14719)
*Richard J. Fawley,Renato Cordeiro de Amorim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VoICE is a new framework for generating counterfactual explanations in feature-weighted k-means clustering, addressing the challenges posed by unlabeled cluster assignments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for interpretable insights in clustering, similar to those provided by counterfactual explanations in supervised learning, as traditional methods struggle to apply due to the nature of clusters.

Method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation by projecting onto the weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, integrating feature weights and ensuring actionability while constraining extrapolation.

Result: The framework consistently generates valid target-cluster membership across various benchmark datasets, outperforming conventional pairwise baselines.

Conclusion: VoICE effectively provides interpretable counterfactual explanations in clustering, improving upon existing methods and ensuring validity in cluster assignments.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

</details>


### [259] [What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14731)
*Kumar Kshitij Patel,Rustem Islamov,Sebastian U Stich,Aurelien Lucchi,Eduard Gorbunov,Lingxiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes improved convergence guarantees for Local SGD in general convex settings influenced by bounded second-order heterogeneity, providing clearer insights into its effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the incomplete theoretical understanding of local updates in Local SGD under realistic data heterogeneity conditions.

Method: Establishing convergence guarantees and improving lower bounds for Local SGD under bounded second-order heterogeneity.

Result: Demonstrated that the conjectured principle regarding bounded second-order heterogeneity applies to general convex objectives, with upper bounds that are nearly tight.

Conclusion: The findings contribute to a more refined convergence theory for Local SGD and reveal the role of second-order heterogeneity in influencing the performance of client models.

Abstract: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

</details>


### [260] [GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14733)
*Xiangni Tian,Kaixian Yu,Runpeng Dai,Niansheng Tang,Hongtu Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces GAttNHP, a framework for effective temporal event forecasting on TKGs by addressing encoding challenges, mutual event influences, and heavy-tailed distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting future events on temporal knowledge graphs is complex due to encoding difficulties, mutual influences between events, and unreliable predictions from sparse, heavy-tailed time intervals.

Method: The GAttNHP framework includes a self-attention encoder for representing chains as point processes, a semantic soft-grouping module for efficient excitation sharing, and a Non-Crossing Quantile regression for stable time predictions.

Result: GAttNHP outperforms state-of-the-art models on six benchmark datasets in both entity and time prediction, especially excelling in long-tail event chains.

Conclusion: The framework's design effectively resolves key challenges in TKG forecasting, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing methods.

Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

</details>


### [261] [ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14770)
*Xuemeng Liu,Zhengpin Li,Wanpeng Tang,Haotong Xie,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces ChronoQG, a benchmark framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), aiming to create questions that are not only based on graph data but also consider temporal aspects. The results indicate significant challenges in existing methods' ability to maintain temporal validity in questions, highlighting the distinction between traditional KGQG and TKGQG.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing static KGQG benchmarks that do not incorporate temporal contexts, which affects the validity of generated questions related to time.

Method: ChronoQG, a framework that combines a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally accurate questions from knowledge graphs.

Result: The framework yielded four benchmark datasets with 16,011 verified questions, revealing that existing LLM-based KGQG methods struggle particularly with preserving temporal constraints in complex scenarios.

Conclusion: ChronoQG serves as a demanding benchmark for TKGQG, exposing a notable gap between static KGQG approaches and the requirements for temporal question generation.

Abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

</details>


### [262] [Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14817)
*Jakub Paplhám,Willem Waegeman,Eyke Hüllermeier,Vojtěch Franc*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the limitations of current methods for evaluating epistemic uncertainty in machine learning and proposes a new framework for assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve the evaluation of epistemic uncertainty, addressing discrepancies between common metrics and Bayes-optimal decision strategies.

Method: The method involves formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization problem and proving that the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties.

Result: The study finds that standard correlation metrics may not predict operational utility, leading to discrepancies in rankings of methods based on uncertainty evaluation.

Conclusion: The paper concludes by advocating for the assessment of achievable risk, regret, and coverage as a more reliable diagnostic for evaluating uncertainty decomposition in decision-making.

Abstract: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

</details>


### [263] [Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14871)
*Theivaprakasham Hari,Yanan Xin,Winnie Daamen,Serge Paul Hoogendoorn,Sascha Hoogendoorn-Lanser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APAL, an asymmetric loss function, enhances time-series forecasting accuracy for rare demand spikes by penalizing under-predictions and focusing training on peak regions while introducing a peak-critical evaluation protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for accurate predictions in applications where under-prediction risk is significantly greater than over-prediction risk, particularly for rare demand spikes.

Method: The paper introduces the Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL) to penalize under-predictions more and apply higher training weights to peak demand periods; also presents a new evaluation protocol concentrating on tail and peak metrics.

Result: APAL shows improved accuracy in tail predictions and peak timings across multiple datasets and forecasting models, showcasing better handling of peak-prediction challenges compared to traditional methods.

Conclusion: APAL is an effective, model-agnostic approach for enhancing peak-prediction quality in time-series forecasting, addressing operational concerns in demand forecasting.

Abstract: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

</details>


### [264] [PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14877)
*Ali Asadi,Krishnendu Chatterjee,Pavol Kebis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This work addresses the challenge of learning reachability in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs) by relaxing assumptions of shared information and centralized algorithms, achieving positive results for decentralized and private information learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reachability is a fundamental yet challenging objective to learn in reinforcement learning, particularly in turn-based stochastic games where adversarial interactions complicate the learning process.

Method: The authors propose a decentralized learning framework that operates with private information and different algorithms for each player, alongside introducing a game-theoretic measure called Expected Conditional Distance (ECD).

Result: They achieve the first positive results for decentralized and private information learning in TBSGs with reachability goals and establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound.

Conclusion: The findings contribute significantly to the field by demonstrating efficient learning strategies under less restrictive conditions.

Abstract: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

</details>


### [265] [Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14888)
*Robert Graham,Edward Stevinson,Yariv Barsheshat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Finetuning language models can induce broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, even while maintaining general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the impact of finetuning on language models with a focus on ideological shifts and generalization across topics.

Method: Finetuning GPT-4.1 with curated ideological datasets and assessing shifts via few-shot prompting and evaluation across varied domains.

Result: Finetuning led to significant ideological shifts on topics like criminal justice and environmental issues, mirroring training data ideologies.

Conclusion: Ideological generalization occurs with finetuning, intensifying shifts and producing extreme outputs, highlighting risks in deploying specialized models.

Abstract: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

</details>


### [266] [Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14895)
*Yu-Du Feng,Niels Mündler-Sasahara,Mark Vero,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This work improves reasoning language models (RLMs) performance by efficiently utilizing unused supervised fine-tuning data, enhancing capabilities in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of enhancing RLMs in domains lacking reliable verifiers, utilizing large amounts of available supervised fine-tuning data.

Method: The authors employ classic instruction tuning combined with merging an instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover reasoning behavior.

Result: The approach shows significant performance improvement in both verifiable and unverified domains such as coding and text summarization, while maintaining performance across other areas.

Conclusion: The proposed method is cost-effective, achieving improvements for under USD $3.

Abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

</details>


### [267] [Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14889)
*Jean-Marc Brossier,Olivier Lafitte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a method for optimizing the linear combination of binary classifiers using truth tables, focusing on unique solutions for empirical risk minimization and explicit weight formulas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the performance and robustness of binary classifiers by combining them optimally based on their classification outcomes.

Method: Utilizes truth tables to organize the dataset, analyzes convexified empirical risk, and derives conditions for uniqueness of solutions. Provides explicit analytical formulas for weights with Exponential and Logistic loss functions.

Result: Establishes sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the minimum point of empirical risk; lists configurations for three classifiers leading to various solution types; derives explicit weights.

Conclusion: Introduces $φ$-frontiers for assessing classifier stability and data quality, offering a structured approach to optimize classifier performance.

Abstract: This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

</details>


### [268] [A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14937)
*Christoph Jürgen Hemmer,Florian Plaswig,Daniel Durstewitz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents DynaBase, a simplified model for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems that achieves competitive performance while minimizing complexity, allowing for more interpretable forecasts and efficient training strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To uncover the minimal requirements for in-context learning in dynamical systems and simplify existing foundation models like DynaMix.

Method: DynaBase is an interpretable two-parameter model that blends the current latent state with in-context neighbors. It structurally reduces DynaMix to its essentials.

Result: DynaBase produces competitive zero-shot reconstructions across various dynamical systems with a significantly reduced parameter count and allows for optimization on prediction measures.

Conclusion: DynaBase reveals essential mechanisms for zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction and provides clarity on training strategies, contributing to a unified understanding of existing models.

Abstract: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

</details>


### [269] [Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14940)
*Phevos Paschalidis,Constantinos Daskalakis,Devavrat Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study presents a method for causal inference in sequential observational settings with outcome interference, utilizing a Markovian framework and Ising model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to address causal inference challenges in scenarios where outcomes are dependent over time and influenced by treatment and latent confounders.

Method: A computationally efficient Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) approach is developed for estimating model parameters under a low-rank factor structure for latent confounders.

Result: Non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation is demonstrated, leading to accurate estimation of causal quantities.

Conclusion: The method is validated through both synthetic data experiments and an analysis of vaccine rates impacting COVID-19 death rates in US counties.

Abstract: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

</details>


### [270] [Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14962)
*Ku Onoda,Paavo Parmas,Hiroki Furuta,Soichiro Nishimori,Yuta Oshima,Shohei Taniguchi,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the limited diversity of images generated by text-to-image models for the same prompt, focusing on improving target-mode coverage through a new reinforcement learning objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enhance the diversity of synthesized images from T2I models, preventing demographic skew and expanding the variety of outputs for given prompts.

Method: Multi-axis max@K is proposed as a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes coverage by weighting samples based on their contribution to maximizing scores across predefined target categories.

Result: The proposed method shows improvement in fairness scores by 0.23-0.36 compared to baseline models, while still preserving image quality and text alignment.

Conclusion: The multi-axis max@K approach effectively enhances target-mode coverage in T2I models, promoting greater diversity in generated images.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

</details>


### [271] [Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14995)
*Sara Ketabi,Matthias W. Wagner,Cynthia Hawkins,Uri Tabori,Birgit Betina Ertl-Wagner,Farzad Khalvati*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), aimed at improving multimodal representation alignment in healthcare by addressing the limitations of traditional Contrastive Learning in medical contexts by incorporating semantic similarities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the inadequacies of traditional Contrastive Learning in medical applications, particularly the false negatives resulting from assumed instance-based correspondence in multimodal datasets.

Method: MseaCL is trained on a pediatric dataset of 3D brain MRI scans and accompanying radiology reports, incorporating semantic similarities to guide learning and reduce the negative impact of similar samples.

Result: The framework achieved significant improvements in downstream tasks, notably a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor classification, indicating enhanced representation quality.

Conclusion: MseaCL demonstrates the potential for achieving more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations, thus enhancing clinical applications in healthcare.

Abstract: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

</details>


### [272] [Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15067)
*Joshua Spear,Matthieu Komorowski,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire,Erica E. M. Moodie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new estimator called Kernel-WIS is introduced for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits, proving to be consistent and superior to existing methods under challenging conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need for accurate off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits using only offline data, highlighting limitations of existing methods.

Method: Kernel-WIS combines the bounded nature of weighted importance sampling with the linear properties of vanilla importance sampling to enhance performance.

Result: Kernel-WIS shows asymptotic consistency and outperforms strong baselines under complex conditions, particularly when the behavior policy is misspecified.

Conclusion: The novel estimator offers significant improvements in off-policy evaluation, demonstrating the potential for more reliable evaluations in practical applications.

Abstract: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

</details>


### [273] [An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15077)
*Yao Cheng Li,Ana Larrañaga,Steven L. Brunton,Urban Fasel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method for engineering problems with poorly characterized governing equations, highlighting its extensions, practical applications, and relevance through two case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of traditional surrogate modeling techniques in capturing the dynamics of engineering systems with limited data and poor interpretability.

Method: The SINDy method utilizes sparse regression over candidate nonlinear terms to recover governing equations from small datasets, with advances including noise-robust and ensembling methods.

Result: The paper presents the SINDy method's effectiveness through case studies on an unmanned aerial vehicle and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger, demonstrating its implementation and flexibility.

Conclusion: SINDy is positioned as a valuable tool for system identification in advanced engineering problems, offering a balance between ease of implementation and versatility.

Abstract: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

</details>


### [274] [Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15080)
*Joshua Spear,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The article examines covariate balance diagnostics to identify hidden confounding in offline reinforcement learning for treatment recommendations, revealing high bias risk and methodological concerns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify and address biases in offline reinforcement learning studies for optimal treatment recommendations, ensuring statistical robustness.

Method: The paper analyzes covariate balance metrics to evaluate their effectiveness in detecting biases in offline RL studies.

Result: Findings indicate a significant risk of bias in current offline RL studies, with existing metrics potentially inadequate for proper assessment.

Conclusion: The authors call for future research to develop more robust methodologies for applying offline RL in treatment recommendations.

Abstract: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

</details>


### [275] [Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15107)
*Sridhar Mahadevan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces LINCS, a categorical framework for addressing non-compositionality in machine learning by reformulating problems as sketches and applying tangent functors.
